extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (examining/prosecuting applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive guidelines for evaluating whether a patent specification satisfies the enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 (and pre-AIA first paragraph). Covers examiner methodology, burdens, examples, and special treatments (e.g., software, biological deposits, amended claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement evaluated against claimed subject matter as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: All questions of enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) are evaluated against the claimed subject matter with the focus of the examination inquiry being whether everything within the scope of the claim is enabled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should determine what each claim recites and what subject matter is encompassed by the claim when the claim is considered as a whole and not analyze the claim elements individually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must establish reasonable basis before rejection for lack of enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: When basing a rejection on the failure of the applicant’s disclosure to meet the enablement provisions of 35 U.S.C. 112(a), USPTO personnel must establish on the record a reasonable basis for questioning the adequacy of the disclosure to enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make and use the claimed invention without resorting to undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite precedent (In re Brown; In re Ghiron). Once USPTO personnel have advanced a reasonable basis, it becomes incumbent on the applicant to rebut that challenge and factually demonstrate the disclosure is sufficient (In re Doyle; In re Scarbrough; see MPEP §§ 2164 - 2164.08(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad functional claims raise enablement concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is not limited to any particular structure for performing a recited function and does not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f), any claim language reciting the ability to perform a function per se would typically be construed broadly to cover any and all embodiments that perform the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such a claim encompasses all devices/structures that perform the function, examiners must be concerned whether the applicant's disclosure sufficiently enables the full scope of protection sought. Examples: In re Swinehart; AK Steel Corp. v. Sollac; In re Moore. Applicants presenting broad claim language must ensure the claims are fully enabled across their scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims scope must be commensurate with scope of enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the claims must be less than or equal to the scope of the enablement provided by the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedent (Sitrick v. Dreamworks; MagSil Corp. v. Hitachi) illustrates that claiming broader subject matter than the specification enables risks invalidity for lack of enablement; examiners should ensure claim scope does not exceed what the spec enables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification need not teach what is well known in the art, but cannot rely on skill in the art to provide novel aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification need not teach what is well known in the art, but applicant cannot rely on the knowledge of one skilled in the art to supply information that is required to enable the novel aspect of the claimed invention when that enabling knowledge is not in fact known in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedent: ALZA Corp., Auto. Techs. Int’l v. BMW, Genentech. Omitting minor details may be acceptable, but omission of any specific starting material or conditions under which a process can be carried out may render undue experimentation necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: High predictability in computer-implemented inventions affects enablement analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For computer-implemented inventions, due to the high level of skill in the art and the similarly high level of predictability, less detailed disclosure may be required to avoid undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2164.08 for examples of computer programming cases and how predictability influences enablement expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must teach how to make and use full scope without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must teach those skilled in the art how to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'scope of enablement' is that disclosed in the specification plus what would be known to one of ordinary skill without undue experimentation. Multiple Federal Circuit decisions reinforce this standard (e.g., Trs. of Bos. Univ.; Sitrick examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for lack of enablement must identify reasons and rely on substantive law
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) must be made when the specification does not enable the full scope of the claim; USPTO personnel should establish a reasonable basis to question the enablement provided and provide reasons for the uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should cite MPEP §§ 2164.01(a) - 2164.08(c) (and § 2164.06(c) for computer programming examples) and provide concrete reasons why the specification does not enable the claimed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement is distinct from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) requires a written description of the invention; this requirement is separate and distinct from the enablement requirement and has the objective of clearly conveying the information that an applicant has invented the subject matter claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description implements the principle that a patent must describe the technology sought to be patented and demonstrates that the patentee was in possession of the invention. See Ariad, Vas-Cath, Univ. of Rochester v. G.D. Searle, Capon v. Eshhar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description: specification must show possession of the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the written description requirement, a patent specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession evidence may include description using words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, reduction to practice, drawings, or distinguishing identifying characteristics. Originally-filed claims or other portions of the original specification may sometimes provide satisfactory description (In re Koller; In re Gardner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession may be shown by deposits for biological materials but deposits do not substitute for written description
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposit of biological material may satisfy written description with respect to a claimed material in certain circumstances, but such a deposit is not a substitute for a written description of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposits must comply with 37 CFR 1.801 et seq. and the written description of the deposited material should be as complete as possible to aid examination and later verification; see Enzo Biochem, In re Lundak, and the Federal Register discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description issues arise in multiple procedural contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about adequacy of written description may arise for original claims, new or amended claims, entitlement to priority dates, or to support claims corresponding to interference counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include LizardTech, Enzo Biochem, Eli Lilly, In re Wright, New Railhead, Tronzo, Fiers, In re Ziegler, Martin v. Mayer, Fields v. Conover. Compliance is a fact-based inquiry resolved case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of adequate written description at filing; examiner initial burden to make prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; the PTO (examiner) has the initial burden, after thorough review, of presenting evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize the disclosure as providing adequate support for the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make a prima facie case, identify the claim limitations not adequately supported and explain why the claim is not fully supported by the disclosure. Example: Hyatt v. Dudas where examiner explained lack of adequate description of a combination even though individual elements were listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: New or amended claims must be supported by original disclosure; new matter prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: The proscription against the introduction of new matter (35 U.S.C. 132 and 251) prevents an applicant from adding information beyond the originally filed subject matter; new or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If originally-filed claims disclose material not found elsewhere in the spec, applicant may amend the spec to include the claimed subject matter (In re Benno). Corrections of obvious errors may be permissible if the ordinary artisan would recognize the error and correction (In re Oda). Guidance on sequencing corrections and reliance on deposits (Cubist Pharm.) and 37 CFR 1.804 requirements apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an essential or critical feature undermines written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can indicate the inventor lacked possession of a broader invention; a claim that omits matter described as an essential or critical feature in the specification does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: PIN/NIP, Gentry Gallery, Johnson Worldwide Assoc. v. Zebco, Tronzo. Such omissions may also give rise to enablement or 112(b) rejections. Examiner should consider statements in the spec that indicate a particular understanding was 'the only possible location' or 'outside the stated purpose.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for examiners: read/analyze spec and identify deficiencies specifically
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should read and analyze the specification for compliance, and, because of the presumption of adequacy, the examiner must present evidence or reasons why the disclosure would not be recognized as adequate by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must identify claim limitations lacking support and explain why; for newly added/amended claims, applicant should be required to point to original-support or amend. MPEP §§ 2163.04, 2163.06 and 714.02 provide further procedural guidance (e.g., a simple statement pointing out lack of support for an amendment may be sufficient when support is not apparent).
